summary:
Murmansk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are prohibited and public expression of gender transition is itself an offence. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 sets out that framework: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and 'extremism' prosecutions. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols, following the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the movement as extremist; criminal prosecutions under that designation carry up to 12 years in prison. A further 81 people across 98 court cases since January 2024 have been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The designation built on the 2013 'gay propaganda' law.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation.

Deaths in custody and physical coercion are documented. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents of Murmansk Oblast live under the same federal statutes as the rest of Russia: the constitution provides no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and legal gender recognition was abolished in 2023 alongside the prohibition on gender-affirming surgery.

Administrative liability applies to displaying alleged movement symbols, most commonly on social media, with 81 people convicted across 98 court cases since January 2024; criminal liability for participation in the designated movement carries up to 12 years. At least 139 people were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports enforcement action, raids, arrests or convictions specifically within Murmansk Oblast; the federal figures cited are national totals and are not broken down by oblast.

Local policing practice, the availability of competent medical care, and the presence or absence of any LGBT+ venues or support organisations in Murmansk city are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk and is a single reported incident; it evidences the practice's existence in Russia but does not establish its prevalence in this oblast.

Whether any entry, screening or document-inspection practice at Murmansk's border crossings specifically targets transgender travellers is not addressed by the inventory.
